name: Question 4
problem:
Find the Laplace transform $Y(s)=L{y(t)}$ if 

$$
{y}^{′}-2y=2{u}_{2}(t)\cdot {e}^{4t-8}\,,\,y(0)=-1,
$$

where ${u}_{2}(t)=u(t-2)$ is the unit step function.

$Y(s)=-\frac{1}{s-2}\,+\,$
{{field-1}},$\,s>4$
worked_solution:
First, we take the Laplace transform of both sides and use the addition and scalar multiplication properties of the Laplace transform:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{y}^{′}-2y} & =L{2{u}_{2}(t)\cdot {e}^{4t-8}} \\ L{{y}^{′}}-2L{y} & =L{2{u}_{2}(t)\cdot {e}^{4t-8}}\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate $L{{y}^{′}},$ we use the formula for the Laplace transform of a derivative and the initial condition $y(0)=1:$

$$
L{{y}^{′}}=sY(s)-y(0)=sY(s)-(-1)=sY(s)+1
$$

To find the transform of the right-hand side, we note that the term 

$$
2{u}_{2}(t)\cdot {e}^{4t-8}
$$

is in the form $u(t-a)\cdot f(t)$ where $a=2$ and $f(t)=2{e}^{4t-8}.$

Now, recall that the second shifting theorem (time-shifting property) states

$$
L{u(t-a)\cdot f(t)}={e}^{-as}\cdot L{f(t+a)}.
$$

  

So, by the second shifting theorem, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{2u(t-2)\cdot {e}^{4t-8}} & ={e}^{-2s}\cdot L{2{e}^{4(t+2)-8}} \\  & ={e}^{-2s}\cdot L{2{e}^{4t}} \\  & ={e}^{-2s}\cdot \frac{2}{s-4} \\  & =\frac{2{e}^{-2s}}{s-4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute these back into our transformed differential equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{y}^{′}}-2L{y} & =L{2{u}_{2}(t){e}^{4t-8}} \\ (sY(s)+1)-2Y(s) & =\frac{2{e}^{-2s}}{s-4} \\ (s-2)Y(s)+1 & =\frac{2{e}^{-2s}}{s-4} \\ (s-2)Y(s) & =-1+\frac{2{e}^{-2s}}{s-4} \\ Y(s) & =-\frac{1}{s-2}+\frac{2{e}^{-2s}}{(s-4)(s-2)}\end{aligned}
$$
